issues.legal_issue: State-owned property situated in a Union Territory is exempt from property taxes imposed under parliamentary authority.
material_facts: The municipal committee assessed property tax on immovable properties owned and occupied by State Governments within a Union Territory.
The States challenged the assessments and demands, claiming the constitutional exemption from Union taxation.
issues.conclusion: The States are exempt from property taxes imposed on their properties in Union Territories under laws made by Parliament.
issues.legal_principle: Article 289(1) exempts State property from Union taxation, and the term “Union Taxation” includes taxes leviable under parliamentary laws applicable to Union Territories, including laws made under Article 246(4). The Court relied on the ratio of In Re The Bill to amend Section 20 of the Sea Customs Act (the Sea Customs case), reaffirmed in Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation v. Income Tax Officer (the APSRTC case), and on the continuity between Section 155 of the Government of India Act, 1935 and Article 289(1).

predicates.constitutional_tax_immunity_appeal: A proceeding challenges a tax assessment on the ground that constitutional immunity protects the property from that tax.
predicates.state_owned_property_in_union_territory: A State Government owns property situated within a Union Territory.
predicates.property_tax_imposed_under_parliamentary: A property tax is imposed in the territory under authority derived from parliamentary law.

issues.definition: When a constitutional tax-immunity appeal concerns State-owned property in a Union Territory taxed under parliamentary authority, the property is exempt from that property tax.

issues.legal_issue: Municipal property taxes imposed in a Union Territory fall within the Union-tax exemption for State property.
material_facts: A municipal committee imposed property tax under a municipal enactment on property owned and occupied by State Governments in a Union Territory.
The municipal enactment directed the collected sums to a municipal fund and assigned municipal functions for collecting and applying those sums.
issues.conclusion: Municipal property taxes imposed in Union Territories are within the exemption in Article 289(1), and State property is exempt from them.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 265, 289(1), 243X and 243ZB, a municipality does not have an independent plenary power to tax; its taxing power is conferred by the relevant legislature. Taxation by authorities within a State is State taxation, while municipal taxes in a Union Territory are within Union taxation. The Court relied on the structure of Articles 285 and 289 and the interpretation of Article 289(1) in the Sea Customs and APSRTC cases.

predicates.constitutional_tax_immunity_appeal: A proceeding challenges a tax assessment on the ground that constitutional immunity protects the property from that tax.
predicates.state_owned_property_in_union_territory: A State Government owns property situated within a Union Territory.
predicates.municipal_body_imposed_property_tax: A municipality imposed a property tax under authority granted by a legislature.

issues.definition: When a constitutional tax-immunity appeal concerns State-owned property in a Union Territory and a municipality imposed property tax on it, that tax falls within the State property immunity.

issues.legal_issue: An ordinary municipal enactment does not impose tax on State property used for trade or business as a law specifying taxable State activities under the constitutional exception to the immunity.
material_facts: The municipal enactment did not specify which trading or business activities of State Governments would be liable to tax.
The enactment was an ordinary municipal law and did not purport to make the policy choice required to identify taxable State activities.
The issue arose in the Court’s consideration of whether tax could be imposed on State property used for trade or business, although that basis had not been advanced by counsel.
issues.conclusion: The municipal enactment cannot be treated as a law under Article 289(2) authorizing tax on State property used for trade or business; those properties are not taxable on that basis under the enactment.
issues.legal_principle: Article 289(2) requires a parliamentary law specifying the trading or business activities of State Governments that may be taxed; the power to tax is not automatic. The Court relied on the relationship between clauses (1), (2) and (3) of Article 289, and on the principle against delegating essential policy choices without legislative guidance from In Re the Delhi Laws Act. It also relied on In Re the Central Provinces and Berar Act and Diamond Sugar Mills Ltd. v. State of U.P. for the limits on using strained interpretations to save legislation, and discussed the difficulty of distinguishing governmental from commercial functions, including New York v. United States and South Australia v. Commonwealth.

predicates.article_289_taxability_appeal: A proceeding considers whether tax may be imposed on State property under an exception to constitutional tax immunity.
predicates.ordinary_municipal_enactment: The tax is imposed under a general municipal enactment rather than a law specifically addressing taxable State activities.
predicates.enactment_does_not_specify_taxable_state: The enactment does not identify which trade or business activities of State Governments are subject to tax.

issues.definition: If a taxability appeal concerns an ordinary municipal enactment that does not identify taxable State business activities, the enactment does not authorize tax on State property used for those activities.

issues.legal_issue: The General Clauses Act definition including Union Territories within the term State does not apply to Article 246, and Union Territories are not equivalent to States for that provision.
material_facts: The dispute required the Court to determine the legislative status of Union Territories and the reach of Parliament’s law-making power there.
The General Clauses Act definition of State had been amended to include Union Territories, while Article 246 separately assigned legislative powers to Parliament and State legislatures.
issues.conclusion: For Article 246, the General Clauses Act definition including Union Territories within State is inapplicable; Union Territories are distinct from States and Parliament has plenary legislative power over them under Article 246(4).
issues.legal_principle: Article 246(4) gives Parliament power to legislate for territories not included in a State, including on matters in the State List. Article 367 and Section 3(58) of the General Clauses Act do not displace that scheme where the definition is repugnant to the subject and context. The Court relied on T.M. Kanniyan v. Income-Tax Officer, Pondicherry and Management of Advance Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Gurudasmal, and considered the differing treatment of Union Territories in Satya Dev Bushahri, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Maula Bux, Ram Kishore Sen and S.K. Singh v. V.V. Giri.

predicates.constitutional_interpretation_proceeding: A proceeding requires interpretation of the constitutional allocation of legislative power.
predicates.union_territory_legislative_status_at_is: The proceeding concerns whether a Union Territory is treated as a State for allocating legislative authority.
predicates.parliamentary_power_over_territory: Parliament has authority to legislate for the territory, including on subjects otherwise assigned to State legislatures.

issues.definition: When constitutional interpretation concerns a Union Territory over which Parliament has legislative authority, the territory is not treated as a State for legislative distribution.
